title.en-US: When the Skies Run Dry: Rain, Rituals, and Rainmaking in Africa3

content.value: The lifeblood of Africa, rain, can be a fickle friend. Droughts grip the land, leaving parched fields and desperate communities. But throughout history, Africans haven't simply waited for the skies to open. From age-old rituals to modern science, a fascinating dance with rain has unfolded. Let's delve into the heart of African rainmaking, exploring traditional practices, the rise of cloud seeding, and the enduring hope for a life-giving downpour.
A Continent Steeped in Rainmaking Traditions

Across Africa, a rich tapestry of rainmaking rituals has been woven. In Mali, the Dogon people perform elaborate dances to appease the ancestors believed to control the rains. Ethiopian Orthodox priests conduct blessings, while Maasai warriors in Kenya offer sacrifices to their deity, Enkai. These practices, passed down through generations, reflect a deep connection to nature and a profound belief in the power of human intervention.
Science Takes the Stage: Cloud Seeding and the Quest for Rain

As scientific understanding grew, so did the search for more pragmatic solutions. Cloud seeding, a technique where airborne particles are introduced into clouds to trigger precipitation, emerged as a potential answer. Countries like South Africa and Morocco have experimented with cloud seeding with varying degrees of success. While the science is still evolving, it offers a glimpse into a future where rainmaking becomes a more technical endeavor.
The Enduring Power of Hope and Tradition

Despite the rise of cloud seeding, traditional rainmaking rituals haven't vanished. They continue to hold a powerful cultural significance, serving as a source of hope and a way to connect with the land and its spirits. In a world increasingly focused on technology, these practices remind us of the enduring power of human belief and the deep connection between humanity and nature.
The Future of Rain in Africa

As climate change casts a long shadow, the quest for reliable rainfall intensifies. Whether through age-old rituals, innovative technology, or a blend of both, Africa's fight for life-giving rain continues. This captivating story is a testament to human ingenuity, our dependence on the natural world, and the enduring hope for a future where the skies deliver their precious bounty.

This project is a simple Next.js example that uses Contentful as a CMS. The project utilizes Next.js Internationalization (i18n) as a UI library, and the content for the pages will be fetched from Contentful.
Let’s go over a few key concepts:

Contentful is a powerful content management platform with an intuitive user interface that allows content managers to create and manage content. It also provides robust APIs for developers to retrieve content and render it in the frontend. Developers create components in the frontend to display the content to end-users.
Next.js is a full-stack React framework that simplifies React development. Developers can use Next.js to create component-driven websites that are highly performant.

: This is the process of showing content to users based on their region. A common use case is writing content in a default language and then translating it into other languages. Locale refers to a language variant specific to a region. For example, German is spoken in both Germany and Austria, but these would have different locales:

: This is the process of ensuring that a website is ready to be consumed across multiple countries and regions. It involves detecting a user’s preferred language automatically in the frontend and using that information to fetch localized content from the content platform.

When building websites, you will create pages, and each page will have components. For example, a hero banner component might display a headline, some body text, and a button or two. You can easily search for "hero banner component" online for more context.

When working with a content platform like Contentful, we need to create a page and then add components inside that page. For the hero banner component, we would create a content type for the page and a content type for the hero banner. Then, we link them together. This process is repeated for other components.
Content modeling is an art in itself, and Contentful’s learning center has a lot of training and even live sessions on this topic. Feel free to check that out.
For this project, I’ll focus on four content types that I’ve created:
With these, I can create a page with a few content entries representing a hero banner and a CTA.
After content modeling and creating the content, I need to make API calls to Contentful to retrieve the content and render it. To do that, I need API keys, which I can get in Contentful under
Since I’m using Next.js, I have to follow some patterns specific to it. You can read more about Next.js
Next.js uses file-based routing, so if I want to have a few pages on my website, each page will have an ID that I can use in the URL. For example, let’s say my website is
, and I want three pages: the homepage, the about page, and the contact page. I’ll create a dynamic route in Next.js using a field property (e.g., “slug”) from my page content type as a unique ID.

Contentful has a built-in slug generator, which makes it easy to set this up in the landing page content type. In Next.js, I define a dynamic route using the slug as the ID so that I can go to Contentful and fetch the content for any page based on the provided slug.
So, my pages would look like this:
But there’s more to it. I also want to internationalize my site, so I’ll have different locales for the pages. For example, the about page would look like:

To implement this, I create a dynamic route using “locale” as the unique ID for each route. When a user visits the site, I need to either automatically redirect them to the correct locale or allow them to pick their language, or even do both.
Most internationalized websites have a locale/language switcher, usually located in the footer. We can implement that as well.
I won’t go into the details of the implementation here, but this is done using Next.js middleware, where I can intercept requests and redirect them to the appropriate locale.
is responsible for rendering the page. I need to retrieve the locale and the slug (e.g., locale: “de”, slug: “about”) and use that to request content from Contentful.
To communicate with Contentful from the frontend, I need to install the JavaScript Contentful client library. I can then create a client. Contentful has two key APIs for content retrieval:
, which can fetch both published and unpublished content (more on the preview later)
I can create two client instances—one for delivery and one for preview—by passing the respective API keys to each.
Contentful's JavaScript client library has a method called
, which retrieves content entries. This method can accept some options, like passing the slug and an include count to retrieve related content in a single query.
The data I get back from Contentful can then be rendered in the frontend.

content.value: Unlike traditional iced coffee (which is simply hot coffee poured over ice), cold brew is crafted through a slow extraction process using cold or room temperature water. This patient approach—typically 12-24 hours—creates a concentrate that's naturally sweeter, less acidic, and incredibly smooth. Mastering Cold Brew Coffee: Recipes for the Perfect Summer Refreshment

There's something magical about that first sip of cold brew coffee on a warm day. Smooth, refreshing, and delightfully low in acidity, cold brew has transformed from a coffee shop specialty into a home brewing essential. Whether you're a cold brew novice or looking to elevate your existing recipes, this guide will walk you through everything you need to create café-quality cold brew in your own kitchen.

Unlike traditional iced coffee (which is simply hot coffee poured over ice), cold brew is crafted through a slow extraction process using cold or room temperature water. This patient approach—typically 12-24 hours—creates a concentrate that's naturally sweeter, less acidic, and incredibly smooth. The result is a versatile coffee base that can be customized in countless ways.
Let's start with the foundation—a perfect cold brew concentrate that serves as the base for all our recipes.
1 cup (100g) coarsely ground coffee (medium-dark roast recommended)
Combine coffee grounds and water in your container, stirring gently to ensure all grounds are saturated
Cover and let steep at room temperature for 12 hours (or overnight)
For a stronger brew, extend to 18-24 hours
Strain through a fine mesh strainer lined with cheesecloth or a paper filter
Store your concentrate in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks
To serve, dilute with equal parts water or milk, pour over ice, and customize to taste.
Beyond the Basics: Creative Cold Brew Variations
Transform your basic brew with warm, aromatic spices.
Combine all ingredients in a glass, stir well, and enjoy this comforting twist on traditional cold brew.
For a tropical vacation in a glass, this recipe delivers creamy indulgence.
Sweetener to taste (coconut sugar works beautifully)
Mix cold brew with coconut milk, stir in coconut cream until dissolved, add sweetener, and pour over ice. Top with toasted coconut flakes for an Instagram-worthy finish.
This barista favorite offers a refreshing, effervescent alternative to cream-based recipes.
Orange or lemon slice for garnish
Fill a glass with ice, pour in cold brew concentrate, top with tonic water, and garnish with citrus. The result is surprisingly complex—bitter, sweet, and refreshing all at once.
Use a higher coffee-to-water ratio (1:3 instead of 1:4) or extend your brewing time.
Simply dilute with more water or milk when serving.
Your grind might be too fine. Adjust to a coarser grind next time, or reduce your brewing time.
Double-filter your concentrate using a paper coffee filter after the initial straining.
Add fresh mint leaves and a splash of lemonade for a refreshing twist
Incorporate pumpkin spice syrup and a dash of nutmeg
Mix with hot chocolate for a cold brew mocha
Infuse with lavender syrup and a touch of honey

While you can make excellent cold brew with basic kitchen tools, dedicated cold brew makers can simplify the process. Look for systems with fine mesh filters, airtight storage capabilities, and easy-pour spouts. Popular options include the Toddy Cold Brew System, Hario Mizudashi, and County Line Kitchen's Mason Jar Brewer.

Cold brew coffee offers endless possibilities for customization while maintaining its signature smooth character. By mastering the basic concentrate recipe and experimenting with creative variations, you'll discover your perfect cup while saving money on coffee shop visits. Remember that cold brew is all about patience—the slow extraction process rewards you with a superior coffee experience that's worth the wait.
What's your favorite cold brew recipe? Start with our suggestions and then let your creativity flow as you craft your perfect summer coffee companion.
